etymology: From lowly + -ness; Old English root, “low in position or estimation.” Renders the Greek tapeinophrosunē, “lowliness of mind,” and the Hebrew ‘ānāvāh, “humility, lowliness.”
biblical_def: Lowliness is the inward disposition of the soul that does not exalt itself—the settled lowliness of mind that takes the lower place willingly, esteems others better than self, and walks softly before God. Paul names it as the very first virtue of the Spirit-shaped life in Ephesians 4:2: with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; he commands it in Philippians 2:3 in pointed contrast to its opposites: let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves; he frames his own ministry in Acts 20:19 as serving the Lord with all humility of mind—the same root word. Christ Himself names lowliness as the inward shape of His own heart and the rest He offers the weary: take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Lowliness is therefore not merely modesty of bearing or softness of voice; it is the inner disposition that has accepted its true place under God and among men, that does not need to be seen, recognized, deferred to, or ranked first, and that finds rest precisely in the lower seat. The opposite, the high-minded soul, is restless because its place is never high enough; the lowly soul is at rest because the place it has accepted is the place its Master held first. Lowliness is the soil in which every other Christian virtue grows: the lowly are teachable (the proud are not); the lowly are forgivable and forgiving (the proud cannot ask pardon and cannot extend it without condescension); the lowly are usable by God (God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble); and the lowly bear the image of the Christ who, being in the form of God, took upon Himself the form of a servant and was found in fashion as a man.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LOWLINESS as humility; freedom from pride; lowness of mind or condition; in scripture, the humble disposition that becomes a follower of Christ.
webster_full: LOWLINESS, n. — 1. Freedom from pride; humility; humbleness of mind. Walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness (Eph 4:1-2). 2. Lowness of condition or rank.
LOWLY, a. — 1. Having a low esteem of one’s own worth; humble; meek; free from pride. 2. Low; not high or lofty; not elevated in place. 3. Low in rank; humble in condition; mean.
scriptures: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
I therefore...beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love.
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations...
corruption_summary: Lowliness is corrupted by the false-humility performance that displays the outward token of low estimation while jealously guarding the inward sense of superiority—and by the assertiveness register of the age that despises lowliness as weakness and refuses the lower seat altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Performed false humility is the most pervasive contemporary corruption of lowliness. The believer learns to display the outward markers of low estimation—the deflection of compliments, the visible self-deprecation, the boast disguised as confession—while the inward sense of superiority remains untouched and even reinforced by the social credit the performance earns. Scripture is sharper than this. Lowliness is the inward disposition, not the outward performance; it is what the heart actually thinks of itself before God, not what the mouth says about itself before men. The cure is the inward work: confess what is actually true, take the lower seat in reality, esteem others better in fact, refuse the inward boast that the performance was meant to mask. The Christ who is meek and lowly in heart is the model: real lowliness, all the way through, with no calculation about the appearance.

The opposite corruption is the assertiveness-culture register that despises lowliness as weakness. The believer is told from every corner to assert himself, to lean in, to know his worth, to refuse the lower seat, to never apologize, to never be made small. The Christ-shaped lowliness Paul commands in Philippians 2 sounds, to such ears, like the relic of a backward and crushing era. But the inversion is not optional Christianity; it is the inner shape of the kingdom and the imitation of the King who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers both the freedom and the dignity of the lower seat: the freedom from the exhausting labor of self-promotion and the dignity of walking the road his Master walked—a road that ends not in obscurity but in exaltation, in due time, by the very hand under which the soul learned to be low.
roots_summary: Greek tapeinophrosunē (lowliness of mind) and Hebrew ‘ānāvāh (humility, lowliness)—the settled inward disposition of the soul that takes the lower place willingly, in imitation of the Christ who is meek and lowly in heart.
roots_lines: Greek tapeinophrosunē (G5012) — lowliness of mind, humility (Eph 4:2; Phil 2:3; Acts 20:19; Col 3:12; 1 Pet 5:5).
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — low, lowly, humble (the adjective; used of Christ’s heart in Matt 11:29).
Hebrew ‘ānāvāh (H6038) — humility, lowliness (Prov 15:33; 18:12; 22:4; Zeph 2:3).
Hebrew ‘ānāv (H6035) — lowly, humble (the adjective; the meek and lowly poor of the Psalms).
usage: I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls—the inward disposition of Christ is the rest He offers to weary souls.
Lowliness is the soil in which every Christian virtue grows; the proud are unteachable, unforgivable, and unusable.
Performed false humility displays the token without the disposition; assertiveness-culture refuses the disposition altogether; biblical lowliness is the inward thing, all the way through.

etymology: From tender, from Latin tener, “soft, delicate, young.” Renders the Greek eusplagchnos, “tender-hearted” (Eph 4:32; 1 Pet 3:8), and the Hebrew imagery of the bowels (rachamim) as the seat of the deepest compassions.
biblical_def: Tenderness is the soft-hearted disposition that is moved by the troubles, weaknesses, and sorrows of others—the inward softness that responds with compassion rather than indifference, with mercy rather than harshness, with the embrace rather than the cold shoulder. The biblical word-pictures are bodily: the Hebrew rachamim locates the deepest compassions in the bowels (the body’s soft inward core), and the Greek eusplagchnos means literally good-of-the-inward-parts—the very organ of feeling rightly disposed toward others. Paul commands tenderness as a mark of Christian community: and be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. Peter commands it in the same register: finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous—be pitiful there renders the same root: be tender-hearted. The supreme model is the LORD Himself, whose tender mercies (rachamim) are great, whose compassions fail not, and who as a father pitieth his children. Christ’s ministry is saturated with the tender disposition: He was moved with compassion at the multitudes as sheep without a shepherd, He wept at Lazarus’s tomb, He had compassion on the widow of Nain, He looked upon the rich young ruler and loved him, He took the children in His arms and blessed them, He gathered Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her chickens. Tenderness is therefore no temperamental softness opposed to the truth; it is the affection of the regenerate heart toward fellow image-bearers and especially toward fellow saints, modeled on the very heart of God in Christ. The hard-hearted believer is a contradiction in terms; the church that has lost its tenderness has lost something essential to its likeness to Christ.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TENDERNESS as the state of being tender; softness; susceptibility of the softer passions; sensibility; readiness to feel for others; in scripture, kind affection toward others.
webster_full: TENDERNESS, n. — 1. The state of being tender; softness; sensibility. 2. Susceptibility of the softer passions; sensibility; readiness to feel for others. 3. Kind attention; anxious care; mildness. 4. Soreness; as, the tenderness of a wound.
TENDER-HEARTED, a. — Having great sensibility; susceptible of the softer passions; easily affected by the sufferings of others; full of pity, compassion, or kindness.
scriptures: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.
Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous.
It is of the LORD’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
corruption_summary: Tenderness is corrupted by the hard-edged, online-debate register of much contemporary Christian discourse that prizes clarity and combat over compassion—and by the inverse sentimentality that detaches tenderness from truth and produces a soft-hearted affirmation that is no longer Christian love.
corruption_paragraphs: Much contemporary Christian discourse, especially in the online register, has hardened into a posture in which clarity, contention, and the scoring of points have crowded out tenderness. The brother in error is dispatched with a clip and a tweet; the wounded saint is met with a critique rather than an embrace; the visible Christian persona is sharp-edged, debate-shaped, and effective at combat but has lost the inward softness that the apostles command and the LORD Himself models. Scripture refuses the choice. Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted: the same Paul who contends earnestly for the faith commands a tender-hearted disposition within the body and toward the world. Recover the doctrine, and the contender for truth recovers also the affection toward persons that the truth was given to serve. The Christ who overturned the tables in the temple is the same Christ who took the children in His arms; the apostle who withstood Peter to his face is the same apostle who wept over his Jewish kinsmen and could call the Galatians my little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you.

The opposite corruption is sentimentality: tenderness detached from truth, the soft-hearted affirmation that cannot speak the hard word the soul needs, the compassion-without-correction that loves the sinner so vaguely it never disturbs his sin. This too is not biblical tenderness. The LORD whose tender mercies are over all his works is the same LORD who hates iniquity and chastens the sons He loves; the Christ who wept over Jerusalem is the same Christ who pronounced its judgment; the apostle who is tender-hearted in Eph 4:32 is the apostle who in the previous chapter exposes the works of darkness. Recover both ends. The biblical Christian is hard-hearted toward sin and tender-hearted toward sinners; firm in truth and soft in spirit; willing to contend and quick to embrace. The two together are what the New Testament means by tenderness, and the church saturated with that double disposition looks more like its Lord than either the hard-edged contender or the sentimental affirmer.
roots_summary: Greek eusplagchnos (good-of-the-inward-parts, tender-hearted—Eph 4:32; 1 Pet 3:8) and Hebrew rachamim (compassions, tender mercies, located in the bowels)—the soft-hearted disposition of the regenerate soul, modeled on the heart of God in Christ.
roots_lines: Greek eusplagchnos (G2155) — tender-hearted, compassionate (literally “good-of-the-inward-parts”); Eph 4:32; 1 Pet 3:8.
Greek splagchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion (the verb of Christ’s repeated compassion in the Gospels).
Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — tender mercies, compassions (the deep-bowels word; plural intensive).
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — loyal love, lovingkindness (the covenant-love word that overlaps with tenderness).
usage: Biblical tenderness is the soft-hearted disposition of the regenerate soul, modeled on the very heart of God in Christ.
The hard-hearted believer is a contradiction in terms; the church that has lost its tenderness has lost something essential to its likeness to Christ.
Hard-edged contention and soft-hearted sentimentality are opposite corruptions; biblical tenderness is firm in truth and soft in spirit, hard toward sin and tender toward sinners.

etymology: From blessed (Old English bletsian, “to consecrate with blood”) + -ness. Renders the Greek makariotēs, “blessedness, happy state,” and the Hebrew ’esher, “happiness, blessedness,” usually in the plural ’ashrē, “O the happinesses of...”
biblical_def: Blessedness, in Scripture, is the deep, settled, God-given state of well-being that belongs to those who stand in the favor of God—not the surface happiness of pleasant circumstances, but the deep happiness of being right with God, walking in His ways, and standing in His covenant favor regardless of outward circumstance. The Psalter opens with the keynote: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly—blessed there is plural in the Hebrew, an exclamation: O the blessednesses of the man! Christ inaugurates His own teaching with a cascade of blessednesses: Blessed are the poor in spirit... Blessed are they that mourn... Blessed are the meek... Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness... Blessed are the merciful... Blessed are the pure in heart... Blessed are the peacemakers... Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake. The Beatitudes invert the world’s rankings: the blessedness Christ pronounces falls on those the world counts unfortunate (the poor, the mournful, the meek, the hungering, the persecuted) precisely because the inward state that meets the world’s pity in the kingdom’s economy meets the Father’s favor. Blessedness is therefore not a circumstance but a state, not a feeling but a standing, not what the man has but what the man is before God. Romans 4 takes up the same word in justification: David also describeth the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. The deepest blessedness is the blessedness of imputed righteousness: the sinner counted righteous in Christ stands in a blessedness no providence can take away, no enemy can touch, no circumstance can erode. The Beatitude register pulls back the curtain on this same blessedness in its practical fruits: the man Christ counts blessed is the man whose inward state has been shaped by the gospel into the conformity to Christ that is itself a foretaste of the consummated blessedness of seeing God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BLESSEDNESS as happiness; felicity; heavenly joys; the favor of God; in a high sense, the blessed estate of those who are justified and reconciled to God.
webster_full: BLESSEDNESS, n. — 1. Happiness; felicity; heavenly joys; the favor of God. Where is then the blessedness ye spake of? (Gal 4:15). 2. The blessed estate of those who are justified and reconciled to God; the felicity of saints and angels in heaven.
BLESSED, ppr. — Made happy or prosperous; rendered favorable; consecrated; pronounced happy; in the highest sense, made eternally blessed, as the saints in heaven.
scriptures: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful. But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.
Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.
corruption_summary: Blessedness is corrupted by the prosperity-gospel reduction that equates it with material flourishing and pleasant circumstances, and by the inverse therapeutic flattening that empties the word to mean only subjective well-feeling rather than the standing-in-God’s-favor that Scripture means.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity-gospel reduction empties blessedness of its biblical depth by re-identifying it with material flourishing and pleasant circumstances. The blessed man, on this account, is the one whose health is excellent, whose finances are abundant, whose family is intact, whose career is ascending. Scripture refuses the substitution at every turn. Christ pronounces blessing precisely on those the world counts unfortunate: the poor in spirit, the mournful, the meek, the persecuted. Paul, sitting in a Roman prison facing execution, writes the most joy-saturated epistle of his career. The man counted by God to be righteous in Christ is blessed even when his body is wasting, his comforts are stripped, and his earthly future is closed; the man whose only blessing is material flourishing is, by Scripture’s judgment, the most pitiable of all (Luke 6:24-26 reverses Christ’s blessings with a corresponding set of woes precisely upon the materially comfortable who have received their reward). Recover the biblical depth, and blessedness recovers its substance: a standing-in-God’s-favor that no providence can erode.

The therapeutic flattening is the contemporary American substitute: blessedness reduced to feeling blessed—the subjective well-feeling that one’s life is going well, that one has things to be grateful for, that the day has gone smoothly. The vocabulary survives; the substance has evaporated. The Bible’s blessedness is objective before it is subjective: the man counted righteous in Christ is blessed whether he feels it or not, and the man whose subjective sense of well-being is high but whose standing before God is unjust is not blessed at all in the biblical sense. The recovery is the recovery of the objective category: blessedness is what one is before God, anchored in imputed righteousness, expressed in the Spirit-wrought Beatitude virtues, and consummated in the seeing-God of the pure in heart. Subjective gratitude is its proper fruit, not its substance; circumstances are its incidental setting, not its definition; the standing-in-God’s-favor that comes by grace through faith in Christ alone is its inalienable root.
roots_summary: Greek makariotēs (blessedness) and makarios (blessed); Hebrew ’esher / ’ashrē (happiness, blessedness, “O the happinesses!”)—the deep, settled, God-given state of well-being that belongs to those standing in His favor in Christ.
roots_lines: Greek makarios (G3107) — blessed, happy (the Beatitude word; James 1:12, 25; Rev 1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7, 14).
Greek makariotēs (G3108) — blessedness (Rom 4:6, 9; Gal 4:15).
Hebrew ’esher / ’ashrē (H835) — happiness, blessedness; the exclamatory plural opening Ps 1, 32, 41, 112, 119, 128.
Hebrew bārak (H1288) — to bless (the related verb, of pronouncing or conferring blessing).
usage: Blessedness is objective before it is subjective—a standing in God’s favor, not a feeling about one’s circumstances.
The Beatitudes invert the world’s rankings: the blessed are those the world counts unfortunate, because the inward states the gospel produces are the very things the Father’s favor rests upon.
Prosperity-gospel reduction equates blessedness with material flourishing; therapeutic flattening reduces it to well-feeling—both miss the standing-in-Christ that is its substance.

etymology: From upright (Old English upriht, “straight up”) + -ness. Renders the Hebrew yōsher, “straightness, uprightness,” from yāshar, “to be straight, level,” and the Greek euthutēs, “straightness.”
biblical_def: Uprightness is the moral quality of being straight before God—a life lived along the line of what is right, true, and just, without crookedness, deceit, or deviation. The Hebrew imagery is geometric: the upright life is the straight line, the plumb-line standard, the road that does not bend. The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them; he that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known; the just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him. Job is described by God Himself as a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil. David prays in his coronation, I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way... I will walk within my house with a perfect heart; and again, let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee. The Psalter’s great word for the people of God is the upright: the upright shall dwell in thy presence; good and upright is the LORD: therefore will he teach sinners in the way; light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart. Uprightness is not sinless perfection—Scripture never claims that for any but Christ—but it is the settled direction of the life: the heart aimed straight at God, the conscience kept sensitive, the path corrected when it bends, the integrity that aligns the inward and outward man so that what the believer is in private and what he is in public are the same man. The upright life is therefore the practical fruit of the heart made new by the gospel: regeneration produces a new direction, and the new direction is straightness—the long arc of a life lived under God’s eye, in the plumb-line of His revealed will, with the integrity that makes the believer a single man before God and his neighbor and not a double-souled creature whose private life contradicts his public profession.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UPRIGHTNESS as perpendicular erection; in morals, integrity in principle or practice; honesty; rectitude of mind and conduct; freedom from deceit or perversity.
webster_full: UPRIGHTNESS, n. — 1. Perpendicular erection. 2. In morals, integrity in principle or practice; honesty; rectitude of mind and conduct; freedom from deceit or perversity. Let integrity and uprightness preserve me (Psa 25:21). 3. Honesty; consistent and straightforward dealing; opposed to deceit, fraud, and crookedness.
UPRIGHT, a. — 1. Erect; perpendicular to the plane of the horizon. 2. Adhering to rectitude in all social intercourse; not deviating from correct moral principles; honest; just; pure.
scriptures: Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee.
He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known.
And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?
Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.
corruption_summary: Uprightness is corrupted by the double-life pattern of the present age in which the public profession and the private practice are different lives entirely—and by the brittle moralism that mistakes external scrupulosity for the inward integrity that aligns the whole man before God.
corruption_paragraphs: The double-life pattern is the most common contemporary corruption of uprightness. The believer maintains the public profession of faith—present at services, present in conversation, present in the categories of self-identification—while the private life (the screen-history, the inward thought-life, the secret habits, the relationships hidden from oversight) tells a different story. The two lives never integrate. The inward and outward man are different men. Uprightness as Scripture means it is the precise opposite: the integrity that aligns the inward and outward, so that what the believer is in private and what he is in public are the same man. The recovery is not better performance of the public life but the bringing of the private life into the light: confession to a brother, accountability, the deliberate work of integrating what has been split. The upright man walks surely because his life is one piece; the double man, even when his public life is impressive, walks unsurely because the foundations are riven.

The opposite corruption is brittle moralism—the external scrupulosity that mistakes itself for uprightness while the heart is unchanged. The Pharisees were the textbook case: outwardly meticulous about every fringe and tithe and ceremonial detail, inwardly full of extortion and excess, whitewashed sepulchers beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within. The Christ who diagnoses them sets the contrast: the upright man is upright at the level of the heart first, with the outward life flowing as the proper fruit of the inward, not painted on as the substitute for it. Recover the inward primacy, and uprightness recovers its substance: a heart aimed straight at God by the regenerating Spirit, with the outward life lived consistently along that aim, in a single integrity that is the long arc of a life lived under God’s eye and pleasing in His sight.
roots_summary: Hebrew yōsher (straightness, uprightness) and yāshar (to be straight, level); Greek euthutēs (straightness)—the moral straightness of the heart-aimed life, integrating the inward and outward man into a single integrity before God.
roots_lines: Hebrew yōsher (H3476) — straightness, uprightness (Job 33:23; Ps 25:21; Prov 2:13; Eccl 12:10).
Hebrew yāshar (H3477, adj.) — straight, right, upright; the great Old Testament moral adjective.
Hebrew yāshar (H3474, vb.) — to be straight, level, right.
Greek euthutēs (G2118) — straightness; Heb 1:8 of the scepter of God’s kingdom.
usage: He that walketh uprightly walketh surely—integrity gives the surefooted gait that the double life can never sustain.
Uprightness is not sinless perfection but the settled direction of the life: the heart aimed straight at God, with the inward and outward man integrated into a single integrity.
Double-life pattern and brittle moralism are opposite corruptions; biblical uprightness is heart-deep and life-wide, the long arc of a man living under God’s eye.

etymology: Old English wiht, “weight, value.” In Scripture chiefly renders the Hebrew kābōd, “weight, heaviness,” whose substantival use becomes the great word glory—the manifested weight of God; and the Greek baros, “weight, heaviness,” used by Paul in 2 Cor 4:17 of an “eternal weight of glory.”
biblical_def: Weight in Scripture is one of the deepest theological metaphors, governing two great clusters of doctrine. First, the glory of God: the Hebrew kābōd literally means “weight, heaviness” before it means “glory.” God’s glory is His manifested weight: the substantial, awe-evoking, ungainsayable substance of who He is, breaking forth in such manifestations as Sinai’s thunder and the cloud filling Solomon’s temple. To glorify God is to give Him weight; to despise Him is to count Him light. The created world is, in Scripture’s view, drained of weight when God is taken out of it: vanity of vanities, all is vanity—the Hebrew hebel, “vapor, breath, lightness,” the opposite of kābōd. To live coram Deo is to live among weighty things; to live as if God were not is to live among vapors. Second, the eschatological weight: Paul in 2 Cor 4:17 sets the present afflictions against a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. The Greek is striking—aionion baros doxes, an eternal heaviness of glory—and the contrast is decisive. The afflictions are light (elaphron, light in weight) and but for a moment; the glory is heavy and forever. The believer’s present troubles, however heavy they feel, are revealed in the eschatological scales as light; the coming glory, however invisible now, is revealed in the same scales as heavy beyond comparison. The weight category therefore organizes much of Christian wisdom. The saint learns to value things by their weight: God Himself heaviest, the soul heavier than the body, eternity heavier than time, the praise of God heavier than the praise of men, the reward of the Father heavier than the rewards of the world, the unseen heavier than the seen. The trained spiritual judgment is, in part, the recovered capacity to feel the true weight of what God has weighted heavily and the true lightness of what He has weighted lightly—and to live accordingly.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WEIGHT as the quantity of a body, ascertained by the balance; heaviness; gravity; that property by which heavy bodies tend toward the center of the earth; figuratively, importance; consequence; moment; pressure.
webster_full: WEIGHT, n. — 1. The quantity of a body, ascertained by the balance; the quality of being heavy. 2. Heaviness; gravity; that property by which heavy bodies tend toward the center of the earth. 3. Pressure; burden; as the weight of grief. 4. Importance; consequence; moment; impressiveness; power; as, men of weight in society. 5. In scripture, glory; as, an eternal weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17).
WEIGHTY, a. — 1. Having great weight; heavy; ponderous. 2. Important; momentous; as, weighty considerations.
scriptures: For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.
And he said, I beseech thee, shew me thy glory.
Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
corruption_summary: The biblical category of weight is corrupted by the lightness culture of the digital age, in which the trained capacity to feel what God has weighted heavily (Himself, the soul, eternity) and what He has weighted lightly (this world’s rewards, the praise of men, the moment’s afflictions) has been progressively dulled by a constant stream of trivializing inputs.
corruption_paragraphs: The digital age is, in many of its tendencies, the systematic dulling of the soul’s capacity to feel weight. The endless scroll trains the attention to flit from item to item, holding each only briefly, weighting nothing for long; the entertainment register makes the soul accustomed to lightness and uncomfortable with anything heavy; the constant access to trivia drains the spaces in life that previously held weighty considerations (death, eternity, God, the soul) and fills them with the immediate-but-trivial. The believer absorbs the cultural training and brings it to the things God has weighted most heavily, finding himself unable to feel the weight of God Himself, the weight of his own soul, the weight of eternity, the weight of the afflictions of the persecuted, the weight of the souls of the lost. Recover the weight category, and the saint begins to recover the spiritual judgment that lives toward God: God heaviest, the soul heavier than the body, eternity heavier than time, the unseen heavier than the seen.

The discipline of recovery is partly negative and partly positive. Negatively: identify and reduce the lightening inputs—the trivial media, the constant distraction, the perpetual stream of items too small to weight. Positively: deliberately spend time with the heavy things—sustained reading of Scripture, especially the weighty books (Romans, Hebrews, Isaiah, the Psalms); sustained meditation on God’s attributes; sustained reflection on death and eternity; sustained prayer that gives the soul time to feel what it is asking; sustained presence with the dying, the bereaved, the persecuted, whose lives are heavy with realities the comfortable believer has trained himself not to feel. The recovery of weight is the recovery of the capacity Paul exercises in 2 Cor 4:17: to feel that present afflictions, however severe they seem, are light and but for a moment, and that the coming glory, however invisible, is a far more exceeding and eternal weight. To live in those scales is to live in the kingdom’s register and to find the daily life ordered accordingly.
roots_summary: Hebrew kābōd (weight, heaviness; the great word that becomes glory) and kābēd (to be heavy, weighty); Greek baros (weight, heaviness; 2 Cor 4:17, “eternal weight of glory”) and doxa (glory; the NT equivalent of kābōd).
roots_lines: Hebrew kābōd (H3519) — weight, heaviness, glory (the great theological substantive).
Hebrew kābēd (H3513) — to be heavy, weighty, glorious (the verb).
Greek baros (G922) — weight, heaviness (2 Cor 4:17, “eternal weight of glory”).
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory (the NT translation of kābōd); inseparable from the weight category.
usage: To glorify God is to give Him weight; to despise Him is to count Him light—the doxological grammar is the weight grammar.
Our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory—the eschatological scales reverse the present sense of weight.

Digital-age lightness dulls the soul’s capacity to feel the true weight of God, the soul, and eternity; recovery is partly negative (reduce trivializing inputs) and partly positive (sustained presence with heavy realities).

etymology: From rejoice + -ing; rejoice from Old French rejouir, “to gladden,” from Latin re- + gaudere (to be glad). Renders the Greek kauchēma, “ground or matter of boasting/rejoicing,” and chara, “joy”; and the Hebrew gīlāh, “rejoicing,” and simchah, “joy.”
biblical_def: Rejoicing is the active habitual expression of the joy that grace has produced in the regenerate soul—not the occasional spike of happy circumstance, but the sustained outgoing of a heart that has found in Christ its supreme treasure and now overflows in praise, gladness, thanksgiving, and even boasting in the Lord. The verb of Philippians is its keynote: rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. The doubling is significant. Paul commands rejoicing not as an emotional state the saint manages to feel but as an act of obedience the saint performs: he rejoices, deliberately, in the Lord, always, even in the Roman imprisonment from which he writes. The grounds of biblical rejoicing are objective: in this ye greatly rejoice—Peter writes—though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ; the rejoicing is anchored in the inheritance reserved in heaven, the salvation ready to be revealed, the trial that perfects faith. Romans 5 names a triple ground of rejoicing: rejoicing in hope of the glory of God, rejoicing in tribulations (because they work patience, experience, hope), and rejoicing in God Himself, through whom we have received the atonement. Paul speaks of my joy and crown, my rejoicing in the Lord, and even I rejoice in the day of Christ. The Beatitude commands rejoicing in persecution: rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven. Habakkuk’s great closing line is rejoicing’s most extreme test: although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines... yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. Rejoicing is therefore the saint’s habitual register, anchored in the unchanging objective grounds the gospel supplies, sustained as an act of obedience even when feelings flag, and present even in tribulation because its sources are not the circumstances but the Lord Himself, the inheritance kept in heaven, and the Christ in whom both have been given.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REJOICING as the act of expressing joy or gladness; the experience of joy or gladness; in scripture, the boasting or glorying which is the proper expression of the saint’s joy in the Lord.
webster_full: REJOICING, n. — 1. The act of expressing joy or gladness. 2. The experience of joy or gladness. 3. The subject or cause of joy.
REJOICE, v.i. — To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations; to exult. Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice (Phil 4:4).
scriptures: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also...
Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines... yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
corruption_summary: Rejoicing is corrupted by the circumstance-dependent register of contemporary faith that rejoices when things go well and falls silent when they do not—and by the manufactured emotional register of certain worship traditions that produces a performance of rejoicing whose intensity has been engineered by music and atmosphere rather than wrought by the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Circumstance-dependent rejoicing is the most common contemporary corruption. The believer rejoices visibly when finances are abundant, health is good, family is intact, the church is growing—and falls silent or grumbles when any of these are removed or reduced. The biblical command is sharper. Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice—and Paul writes this from prison. Rejoice evermore—the apostle commands continual rejoicing without circumstantial qualification. Although the fig tree shall not blossom... Habakkuk takes rejoicing to its most extreme test, the loss of every visible provision, and concludes with a rejoicing that has nothing left to rejoice in but the LORD Himself. Recover the doctrine, and rejoicing recovers its anchorage: not in what is happening to me but in what God has done in Christ, what He has reserved for me, and what He Himself is. The objective grounds do not change with the circumstances; the rejoicing therefore need not change either.

The opposite corruption is the manufactured emotional rejoicing of certain worship traditions, in which the felt-intensity of rejoicing is engineered by music, lighting, atmosphere, and crowd dynamics rather than wrought by the gospel itself. The believer leaves such services emotionally lifted and identifies the lift with rejoicing in the Lord; the engineering is not the same thing. Biblical rejoicing is wrought by the gospel: the truth of what God has done in Christ pressed home to the soul produces a joy that is its proper response, and that joy expresses itself in rejoicing whether musical accompaniment is intense or absent. The recovery is the recovery of the substance: keep the gospel central in worship, preach Christ, lift up the cross, set forth the inheritance, name the grounds of joy—and the rejoicing that responds will be the rejoicing the Bible commands, anchored in what cannot be taken away.
roots_summary: Greek kauchēma (ground/matter of rejoicing or boasting) and chara (joy); Hebrew gīlāh (rejoicing) and simchah (joy)—the saint’s habitual outgoing of gospel-wrought joy in the Lord, anchored in unchanging objective grounds.
roots_lines: Greek chairō (G5463) — to rejoice, be glad (Phil 4:4; 1 Thess 5:16).
Greek kauchēma (G2745) — ground or matter of rejoicing/boasting (Phil 1:26; Heb 3:6).
Greek chara (G5479) — joy, gladness (the noun).
Hebrew gīlāh (H1525) — rejoicing, gladness; cousin of simchah (joy).
usage: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice—Paul writes from a Roman prison; the doubling is deliberate.
Rejoicing is anchored in objective grounds—what God has done in Christ, what He has reserved, and what He Himself is—not in shifting circumstances.
Habakkuk’s closing rejoicing is the verb’s most extreme test: every visible provision removed, the saint still rejoices in the LORD.

etymology: From full + -ness. Renders the Greek plērōma, “that which fills, completion, fulness,” and plousios-family riches-of words; and the Hebrew mālē’, “to be full,” and shalom in its sense of completeness.
biblical_def: Fulness in Scripture is one of the deepest Christological and ecclesiological substantives, governing several great doctrinal claims. First, the fulness of God is in Christ bodily: for it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell; for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The Christ in whom the church places her trust is no diminished mediator but the One in whom the entire divine fulness has taken residence in the incarnation. Second, the fulness of Christ is given to the church: and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all. The church is named in the staggering category of Christ’s own fulness; she is what fills Him out in His mediatorial reign over creation, even as He Himself is full of the Godhead. Third, the church is being grown into the measure of Christ’s fulness: till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ. The fulness already given (in union with Christ) is to be progressively realized in the church’s growth toward the maturity of her Head. Fourth, the fulness of times is the appointed historical hour at which God brought His redemptive purposes to their climax: but when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law; that in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ. History is not random; it ripens to its appointed fulness in Christ. Fifth, the fulness of the Gentiles and of Israel are paired in Rom 11 as the great eschatological ingatherings: blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved. Fulness is therefore the verb of completion brought into substantive form: completion of the divine indwelling in Christ; completion of Christ’s mediatorial body in the church; completion of the church’s maturation into her Head; completion of God’s historical purposes in the appointed hour; completion of the redemptive gathering of Gentile and Jew alike. The fulness category gathers up the whole scope of God’s saving work and sets it forth as the sufficient, complete, exhaustive answer of God to every emptiness sin produced.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FULNESS as the state of being filled so as to leave no part vacant; the state of abounding or being in great plenty; in theology, the entirety of divine attributes dwelling in Christ.
webster_full: FULNESS, n. — 1. The state of being filled, so as to leave no part vacant. 2. The state of abounding or being in great plenty. 3. Completeness; the state of being full or fully completed. 4. Largeness; extent; vastness. 5. In theology, the entirety of divine attributes dwelling in Christ (Col 1:19; 2:9); the completeness of the appointed times (Gal 4:4).
scriptures: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all.
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.
Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of fulness is corrupted, on one side, by the diminished-Christ register of liberal critical scholarship that strips Christ of the divine fulness Colossians explicitly affirms—and on the other by the experiential register that treats fulness of the Spirit as a privileged second-blessing rather than as the ordinary regenerate life applied to the body of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal critical traditions corrupt fulness by stripping Christ of the divine fulness Colossians and Ephesians explicitly affirm. The high Christology of in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily is treated as later theological development to be peeled away from a more modest historical Jesus; the cosmic Christ of the fulness of him that filleth all in all is replaced by a wisdom teacher whose authority is bracketed and whose claims are domesticated. The recovery is the recovery of the text’s plain claim. The Christ the apostles announce is the One in whom the entire divine fulness has taken residence; any diminishment of this Christ is the loss of the Christ the New Testament actually delivers. The fulness category is not a peripheral New Testament idea but a structural one—and stripping it produces a different Christ, a different church, and a different gospel.

The experiential corruption is the treatment of fulness of the Spirit as a privileged second-blessing experience available only to a subset of believers, often marked by particular spiritual phenomena, rather than as the ordinary regenerate life applied to the whole body of Christ. The New Testament does speak of being filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18) and being full of the Holy Ghost (Acts 6:3; 11:24), and these are realities to be sought and known. But the structural category of fulness in Ephesians 1, Colossians 1-2, and Galatians 4 is not a privileged-elite experience; it is the foundational reality of every believer’s union with the Christ in whom all fulness dwells. The recovery is to hold both: the foundational fulness of every believer in Christ (which grounds all assurance), and the practical, daily, ongoing fulness of the Spirit (which is sought, walked in, and to be characteristic of every Christian, not a privileged subset). Both together display the doctrine the New Testament actually teaches—and the church that holds both is the church that knows the sufficient, complete, exhaustive answer of God in Christ to every emptiness sin produced.
roots_summary: Greek plērōma (that which fills, completion, fulness) and the verb plēroō (to fill); Hebrew mālē’ (to be full) and shalom (completeness)—the Christological and ecclesiological category of completion in Christ, by whom all the fulness of God indwells the church through union with Him.
roots_lines: Greek plērōma (G4138) — that which fills, completion, fulness (the great Christological substantive; Col 1:19; 2:9; Eph 1:23; 3:19; 4:13).

Hebrew mālē’ (H4390) — to be full, to fill.

The church is named in the staggering category of Christ’s own fulness—his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all.
When the fulness of the time was come—history ripens to its appointed fulness in Christ; the redemptive hour was not random but ordained.

etymology: From Old French poverte, from Latin paupertas (poverty), from pauper (poor). Renders the Hebrew rīsh, rēsh, “poverty,” and the Greek ptōcheia, “destitution, beggary.”
biblical_def: Poverty in Scripture is treated in two registers, material and spiritual, and the Bible refuses to collapse either into the other. Material poverty is the actual lack of the goods necessary for life—food, clothing, shelter, the means of provision—and Scripture addresses it pastorally with sustained seriousness: the law commanded gleaning and the year of jubilee, the prophets thundered against the oppression of the poor, the wisdom literature counseled both the diligence that ordinarily prevents poverty and the generosity that relieves it, the apostles gathered collections for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and Christ Himself stood for the poor and preached the gospel to them as the credential of His mission. The biblical disposition toward the materially poor is mercy, justice, and active relief; the biblical warnings to the church are sharp against any neglect (whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?). Spiritual poverty—poverty of spirit—is the deeper biblical category, and it is the opening Beatitude: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Spiritual poverty is the inward state of the soul that knows itself bankrupt before God, has no righteousness of its own to plead, is empty of self-righteousness and self-sufficiency, and casts itself entirely upon the grace of God in Christ. It is the very opposite of the Laodicean self-assessment (I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing) and the precondition of every saving response to the gospel: the soul that does not feel its poverty cannot receive the riches of Christ. The two poverties intersect deeply but are not identical. The materially rich may be spiritually poor (Abraham, Joseph, David), and the materially poor may be spiritually rich (the Macedonian saints whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality); but Scripture warns that material wealth disposes the heart toward spiritual self-sufficiency in a way that material poverty does not (how hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!), and that the poor have therefore often heard the gospel more gladly than the rich precisely because their material situation has not insulated them against the diagnosis the gospel makes. The Christ who for our sakes became poor that we through His poverty might be rich (2 Cor 8:9) sums up the doctrine in His own person: the divine emptying that became the church’s eternal riches.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines POVERTY as destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence; figuratively, want of spirit; meanness; defect or deficiency.
webster_full: POVERTY, n. — 1. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence. 2. Barrenness of sentiment or ornament; defect; as, the poverty of a composition. 3. Want; defect; as, the poverty of language. 4. In scripture, that humble state of mind that is sensible of the want of righteousness in oneself, and looks to Christ for it (Matt 5:3).
scriptures: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.
How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
corruption_summary: The biblical doctrine of poverty is corrupted by the prosperity gospel that treats material poverty as a sign of insufficient faith and material wealth as the credential of God’s favor—and by the inverse romanticization of poverty in certain progressive traditions that treats material poverty itself as virtue and obscures the deeper biblical category of poverty of spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel corrupts the biblical doctrine of poverty by reading material wealth as the credential of God’s favor and material poverty as a sign of insufficient faith. The Scripture refuses both ends of this read. The materially poor include Christ Himself (who had no place to lay His head), the apostles (who left all to follow Him and ended their lives in want and martyrdom), the saints of Hebrews 11 (who wandered in deserts and mountains, of whom the world was not worthy), and the Macedonian churches whose deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality. The materially rich include Abraham, Job, Joseph, David, Solomon, Joseph of Arimathea, and Lydia. Material condition is not the measure of God’s favor; the prosperity gospel’s confusion of the two leaves the materially poor saint inappropriately ashamed and the materially comfortable sinner inappropriately confident, and obscures the much more serious diagnostic Scripture actually makes: the danger of riches to the soul precisely because they incline the heart toward the spiritual self-sufficiency that bars the kingdom.

The opposite corruption is the romanticization of material poverty in certain progressive Christian traditions, in which the materially poor are treated as automatically spiritually privileged and the materially comfortable as automatically suspect, with material poverty itself elevated to a kind of virtue. This too is not the biblical doctrine. Material poverty is, in itself, a hardship and a burden that Scripture commands the church to relieve; it is not a virtue, and Scripture nowhere commends it as such. What Christ calls blessed is poverty of spirit—the inward state of bankruptcy before God that casts itself entirely upon the grace of Christ—a state to which the materially poor may have easier access (because their condition has not insulated them against the gospel’s diagnosis) but to which the materially comfortable can equally come if they will hear the diagnosis Revelation 3 makes of the Laodicean condition. Recover both ends. The materially poor are to be relieved; the spiritually poor are to be blessed; the materially rich are warned against the dangers their wealth poses to their souls; and all alike, rich and poor, are called to the poverty of spirit that alone can receive the riches of Christ—the Christ who Himself became poor that all might be made rich in Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew rīsh / rēsh (poverty) and ‘ānī (poor, afflicted); Greek ptōcheia (destitution) and ptōchos (the begging poor)—both the material poverty Scripture commands the church to relieve and the poverty of spirit Christ pronounces blessed at the gate of His kingdom.
roots_lines: Greek ptōchos (G4434) — poor, beggar, destitute (the “poor in spirit” of Matt 5:3).
Greek ptōcheia (G4432) — poverty, destitution (2 Cor 8:2, 9).
Hebrew rīsh / rēsh (H7389) — poverty, want.
Hebrew ‘ānī (H6041) — poor, afflicted, humble (often used of the spiritually poor in the Psalter).
usage: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven—the opening Beatitude diagnoses the inward state of bankruptcy that alone can receive the riches of Christ.
Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich—the divine emptying that became the church’s eternal riches.

Prosperity gospel reads wealth as God’s favor; progressive romanticization reads poverty as virtue; biblical doctrine refuses both and holds material and spiritual poverty in their proper distinct registers.

etymology: From Old French richesse, “wealth, opulence,” from riche (rich). Renders the Greek ploutos, “wealth, riches,” both literal and (chiefly in Paul) of the spiritual riches given in Christ; and the Hebrew ‘ōsher, “riches.”
biblical_def: Riches in Scripture have a material register and a spiritual register, and Paul especially exploits the second to set forth the gospel’s great gifts. Material riches are treated soberly: they are gifts of God when given (the wealth of Abraham, Job, Solomon was from the LORD), they are dangers when held wrongly (they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare; how hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!), they are to be enjoyed with thanksgiving and held with open hands ready to do good and to communicate (1 Tim 6:17-19), and they are nothing in the day of wrath (their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD). The deeper biblical riches—the riches that the New Testament most loves to celebrate—are the spiritual riches given in Christ. Paul names them in tight, jewel-like phrases: the riches of his grace (Eph 1:7; 2:7), the riches of his glory (Rom 9:23; Eph 3:16; Phil 4:19; Col 1:27), the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints (Eph 1:18), the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom 11:33), the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering (Rom 2:4), and the unsearchable riches of Christ (Eph 3:8). The cumulative effect is staggering: God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and the very person of His Son are all, in apostolic vocabulary, riches—wealth bestowed on the church, an inheritance reserved in heaven, a treasure that exceeds every earthly treasure precisely because it cannot be taken away. The supreme contrast text is 2 Cor 8:9: for ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. The Son’s self-impoverishment in the incarnation is the means by which the spiritually bankrupt are made spiritually rich in Him. The saint’s relation to riches is therefore two-edged. He holds material riches lightly when given, generously when shared, and not at all as the measure of his security; and he holds the spiritual riches of Christ as his actual treasure, his unfading inheritance, his exhaustless storehouse, the wealth that no thief breaks through to steal and no rust corrupts.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RICHES as wealth; opulence; affluence; possessions of land, goods, or money in abundance; figuratively, splendid, sumptuous, or expensive things; in scripture, the spiritual blessings and treasures given in Christ.
webster_full: RICHES, n. pl. — 1. Wealth; opulence; affluence; possessions of land, goods, or money in abundance. 2. That which makes rich, as moral or spiritual qualities. 3. Splendid, sumptuous, or expensive things. 4. In scripture, the spiritual blessings and treasures given in Christ; as, the unsearchable riches of Christ (Eph 3:8); the riches of his grace (Eph 1:7); the riches of his glory (Phil 4:19).
RICH, a. — 1. Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods, or money. 2. In scripture, abounding in spiritual gifts; abounding in grace and divine favor.
scriptures: In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.
Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
corruption_summary: Biblical riches are corrupted by the materialist register of the present age that has trained the believer to feel the word as referring chiefly to money—and by the prosperity gospel’s further confusion that uses the apostolic riches-of-Christ language as the warrant for promising material prosperity to the faithful.
corruption_paragraphs: The materialist register of late-modern consumer culture has trained the believer to hear riches as referring chiefly to money, and to read even the apostolic phrases through that lens. Paul’s riches of his grace, riches of his glory, unsearchable riches of Christ, and Philippians 4:19’s my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus, ought to evoke in the saint the staggering wealth of what God has bestowed and reserved in Christ; they often evoke, in the contemporary register, vague hopes of financial provision. Recover the doctrine, and the apostolic phrases recover their proper weight. The riches Paul celebrates are God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and the very person of His Son—treasures the believer can savor with his eyes closed and his bank account empty, and that survive every loss the present life can bring.

The prosperity gospel takes the cultural materialism a step further and uses the apostolic riches-of-Christ language as the warrant for promising material prosperity to the faithful. The verses are quoted; the substitution is performed; the spiritual riches Paul means are conflated with the financial riches the prosperity gospel promises; and the believer is taught to expect that his union with Christ entitles him to material flourishing in this life. Scripture refuses the substitution. Christ Himself had no place to lay His head; the apostles for the most part died in poverty and martyrdom; the saints of Hebrews 11 wandered in deserts; the Macedonian saints’ deep poverty is celebrated alongside the riches of their liberality. The spiritual riches of Christ are real and exhaustless, but they are spiritual—the riches that no thief breaks through to steal—and they do not translate into a divine guarantee of material wealth in this life. Recover both ends. Hold the spiritual riches of Christ in their full apostolic weight; receive material provision with thanksgiving as a gift; hold it with open hands; refuse to confuse the two.
roots_summary: Greek ploutos (wealth, riches) and the verb ploutiō (to enrich); Hebrew ‘ōsher (riches)—both material wealth (gift when given, danger when held wrongly) and the spiritual riches of God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and very person bestowed in Christ.
roots_lines: Greek ploutos (G4149) — wealth, riches (used by Paul of the riches of God’s grace, glory, wisdom).
Greek plousios (G4145) — rich, wealthy (the adjective; 2 Cor 8:9, “though he was rich”).
Greek ploutiō (G4147) — to make rich, enrich (2 Cor 8:9, “that ye through his poverty might be rich”).
Hebrew ‘ōsher (H6239) — riches, wealth (Gen 31:16; Eccl 4:8; Jer 17:11).
usage: The riches Paul celebrates are God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and the very person of His Son—treasures the saint can savor with empty hands and full heart.
Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich—the Son’s self-impoverishment is the means by which the bankrupt are enriched.
Materialism reduces riches to money; prosperity gospel conflates spiritual riches with material wealth; biblical doctrine holds both registers in their proper distinct places.

etymology: Latin triumphus, the Roman victory procession in which a conquering general entered the city behind his vanquished enemies. Renders the Greek thriambeuō, “to lead in triumphal procession” (2 Cor 2:14; Col 2:15), and the Hebrew ‘ālaz, rūa, “to shout in triumph.”
biblical_def: Triumph in Scripture is the public, exultant celebration of victory—and the two great biblical triumphs both belong to Christ. The first is His triumph over the powers of darkness at the cross. Colossians 2:15 sets the picture at its most arresting: and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it. The Greek thriambeuō is the Roman triumph-procession word—the conquering general entering his capital with the vanquished enemies led in chains behind his chariot, the city watching the public display of who had defeated whom. Paul takes the most ironic of all biblical pictures and applies it to the cross: at the moment when, to the watching world, the powers of darkness seemed to be defeating Christ, He was in fact spoiling them, disarming them, and leading them in His own triumphal procession. The crucifixion was the triumph; the cross was the chariot; the principalities and powers were the chained enemies displayed; the resurrection and ascension were the procession’s consummation. The second great triumph is the ongoing triumph of Christ over the world through the spread of the gospel. 2 Corinthians 2:14: now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place. The apostles are pictured as those led in Christ’s ongoing triumphal procession through the world; the gospel they carry is the public proclamation of His victory; the conversions are the visible spoils of His triumph among the nations. The saint’s personal triumphs are derivative of these decisive ones. Christ has triumphed over sin, death, the devil, and the world; the believer triumphs in Christ as he applies that decisive triumph to his own particular battles; this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith; and the consummation will be the full unveiling, at the day of Christ, of the triumph that has been settled since the cross. The biblical disposition toward triumph is therefore unembarrassed celebration of what God has done in Christ, with the personal triumphs of the saints set always inside the great triumph of the King—and the church called to march, in this present age, as those whose Lord has already won.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TRIUMPH as a public exhibition of victory or success; among the Romans, the pomp and ceremonies attending the entry of a victorious general into the city; in scripture, the conquest gained by Christ over the powers of darkness.
webster_full: TRIUMPH, n. — 1. Among the Romans, a pompous ceremony performed in honor of a victorious general, who was allowed to enter the city crowned, originally with laurel, but in later times with gold, bearing a truncheon in one hand and a branch of laurel in the other. He was carried in a chariot drawn by four white horses, and followed by the captives and rich spoils. 2. Joy or exultation for success. 3. Victory; conquest. 4. In scripture, the conquest gained by Christ over the powers of darkness (Col 2:15) and the ongoing triumphal procession of His gospel through the world (2 Cor 2:14).
scriptures: And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place.
For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.

And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war... and he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
corruption_summary: Biblical triumph is corrupted, on one side, by the practical defeatism of the present church that walks as if the cross had not been a triumph and the gates of hell were in fact prevailing—and on the other by the triumphalism of certain dominion-theology traditions that mistake the proper unveiling of Christ’s settled victory for a present-political program of cultural conquest the New Testament does not promise in those terms.
corruption_paragraphs: Practical defeatism is the most pastorally damaging contemporary corruption of triumph. The believer who reads Colossians 2:15 and 2 Corinthians 2:14 in the comfort of his closet often lives in the office, the home, and the public square as if the cross had not been a triumph and the gates of hell were in fact prevailing. The cultural pessimism of the moment, the visible decline of Christian institutions, the apparent retreat of the church before the spirit of the age, all conspire to produce a Christianity that walks like a losing side. Scripture refuses this. The triumph of Christ at the cross is decisive and complete; the ongoing triumph of His gospel through the world is real and continuing; the consummated triumph at the day of Christ is settled and certain. Recover the doctrine, and the saint’s gait changes. He walks in his own particular battles as one whose Lord has already won the war, with the patience and the courage and the unembarrassed celebration that such a settled victory makes possible.

The opposite corruption is the triumphalism of certain dominion-theology and Christian-nationalism traditions that mistake the proper unveiling of Christ’s settled victory for a present-political program of cultural conquest the New Testament does not promise in those terms. The Bible’s triumph is principally Christological (Col 2:15) and gospel-shaped (2 Cor 2:14): the triumph at the cross and the ongoing triumph through the spread of the gospel. The consummation of the triumph is eschatological, at the day of Christ. Between cross and consummation, the church carries the gospel into every nation as the visible spoils of His already-won victory, but the New Testament does not promise that this between-time will be one of unbroken cultural ascendancy for the church; on the contrary, it predicts persecution, tribulation, and the rise of the man of lawlessness, alongside the steady gospel ingathering. Recover both ends. Refuse the practical defeatism that walks as if the cross had not been a triumph, and refuse the triumphalism that mistakes the eschatological hope for a between-time program of cultural conquest. The biblical triumph is decisive at the cross, ongoing through the gospel, consummated at Christ’s return—and the saint marches in the procession of the King who has already won, with the patience and the joy that such a march invites.
roots_summary: Greek thriambeuō (to lead in triumphal procession—Col 2:15; 2 Cor 2:14) and Hebrew ‘ālaz / rūa (to shout in triumph)—the public, exultant celebration of Christ’s decisive triumph at the cross, His ongoing triumph through the gospel, and the consummated triumph at the day of the Lord.
roots_lines: Greek thriambeuō (G2358) — to lead in triumphal procession (only Col 2:15 and 2 Cor 2:14 in the NT, both of decisive importance).
Greek nikaō (G3528) — to overcome, conquer (the related verb of personal triumph in Rev 2-3; 1 John 5:4).
Hebrew ‘ālaz (H5937) — to exult, triumph, rejoice.
Hebrew rūa (H7321) — to shout, raise a war or triumph cry.
usage: Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it—the crucifixion was the triumph; the cross was the chariot.
Always causeth us to triumph in Christ—the apostles are led in Christ’s ongoing triumphal procession through the world.

Practical defeatism walks as if the cross had not been a triumph; triumphalism mistakes the eschatological hope for a between-time program; the biblical triumph holds cross, gospel, and consummation in their proper places.
